why: Edge case: the visible signs point to an external route hijack, but the confirmed cause is an internal configuration change. Tempting wrong labels: routing_bgp (a hijack is mentioned), security, dns (a resolver service), third_party_upstream.

incident.summary: Public resolver service unreachable on plain DNS; service prefixes no longer visible
incident.reported_symptoms: Monitoring alert: query volume to the public resolver service dropped sharply on plain DNS over UDP and TCP and on DNS over TLS. DNS over HTTPS traffic was mostly unaffected.

work_notes.note: Query volume fell sharply on plain DNS and DNS over TLS. DNS over HTTPS is mostly fine, because those clients use a hostname that resolves to different addresses. Our prefixes for the service are no longer visible from external route collectors.

Another network is now originating one of our service prefixes. First thought was a route hijack, but our own advertisements for these prefixes are gone, withdrawn by our routing automation rather than by a peer or a router fault.

Found it: a configuration change made weeks ago for a service that has not launched linked the resolver prefixes to a non-production routing topology. It had no effect until a later update to that service triggered a global refresh, which withdrew the prefixes. The other network's origination only became visible because our advertisements were gone.
Reverted the configuration and started re-advertising the prefixes.
Traffic is recovering, but about a quarter of edge servers dropped the service address bindings when they reconfigured automatically during the outage. Running accelerated reconfiguration on those.
Query volume back to normal globally. The original change was peer reviewed, but this legacy system has no staged rollout or health checks.

resolution.restoration_action: Reverted the faulty configuration, re-advertised the prefixes, and ran accelerated reconfiguration on edge servers that had lost the service address bindings.
resolution.confirmed_cause: A configuration change linked the service prefixes to a non-production routing topology; a later update to the same service triggered a global refresh that withdrew the prefixes.
supporting_evidence: Our advertisements were withdrawn by internal automation after the refresh
Traffic recovered after the revert and re-advertisement
The other network's origination of the prefix was a visible side effect, not the cause
resolution.remaining_uncertainty: None for the cause. The other network's origination of the prefix is being followed up separately.
resolution.follow_up: Retire the legacy routing system in favor of one with staged rollouts and automatic rollback.

why: Expected alert from a planned, one-time maintenance with no impact. Tempting wrong labels: routing_bgp (a BGP session went down), software_firmware_bug (the notice mentions a defect), third_party_upstream (a peering partner did the work).

incident.summary: BGP session to the secondary route server at the exchange went down
incident.reported_symptoms: Monitoring alert: BGP session to the secondary route server at the exchange went down at 12:21 UTC. The session to the primary route server stayed established.

work_notes.note: Alert: BGP session to the secondary route server at the exchange is down. The session to the primary route server is still established and its prefixes are present.

Matches the exchange operator's maintenance notice received a week ago: progressive BGP software upgrade on the secondary route server, expected downtime up to 30 minutes per exchange, 4-hour window booked for about 2 hours of work. The notice asks members to confirm they are connected to the primary route server, which we are.
No traffic impact. Prefix counts and traffic on the primary session are unchanged. Acknowledged the alert. No action needed.
Secondary session re-established at 12:50 on its own. Prefix counts back to normal. Closing.

resolution.restoration_action: None needed; the session re-established on its own after the operator finished the upgrade.
resolution.confirmed_cause: Planned, announced maintenance on the exchange operator's secondary route server.
supporting_evidence: Operator maintenance notice covering this window
Session to the primary route server stayed up throughout
No change in traffic or prefix counts on the primary session
resolution.follow_up: None documented. The notice describes the upgrade as a one-time fix for a software defect.

why: Evidence leans toward hardware (a switch fabric module) but the cause was never established, and a software controller was also misbehaving. Existing category, low confidence, human review needed.

incident.summary: Packet discards and loss on all traffic through a core switch
incident.reported_symptoms: Monitoring alarms at 13:39 UTC showing discards and loss on circuits passing through one core switch, affecting several service layers and one connector customer.

work_notes.note: The SDN controller received a link migration event from the switch. Forced a diff to restore proper forwarding (first re-sync).
Every port on the switch reports discards except ports in slot 1. Network engineering thinks this is a hardware issue. Vendor case opened as priority 1.
Moved IP backbone traffic to alternate circuits. IP traffic is no longer affected. Layer 2 services still are.
Disabled one switch fabric module while working with the vendor.
Another link migration event from the switch. Disabled controller discovery with approval until the event is resolved. Forced re-syncs again at 16:11 and 16:20.
Vendor and our engineers think there may be a switch-fabric issue. Not confirmed.
With director approval, disabled all backbone interfaces. Services with backup paths recovered. Seven customer VLANs with no backup path are still affected.
Rebooted the core switch. Forwarding restored. Brought the admin-down ports back into service.
Re-enabled controller discovery; it is working normally.
Vendor call ended without a root cause.

resolution.restoration_action: Rebooted the core switch and brought the disabled ports back into service.
supporting_evidence: Discards on every port except those in slot 1
Forwarding restored only after the switch reboot
Vendor and engineers suspected the switch fabric, unconfirmed
resolution.remaining_uncertainty: Root cause not established; the vendor was still investigating. The controller also logged repeated link migration events, and neither a hardware fault nor a software cause was confirmed.
resolution.follow_up: Vendor investigation continues. Alarming added for switch fabric module events. A guideline to escalate to disruptive restoration steps sooner is proposed.

why: Certificate expiry has no category in the taxonomy. The classifier should propose a new one for a human to approve. Arguable alternative: missed_maintenance, because a release was not flagged as time-critical. See notes.

incident.summary: HTTPS connections to storage endpoints rejected in all regions
incident.reported_symptoms: Monitoring alert at 20:44 UTC: HTTPS connections to the blob, table, and queue storage endpoints are being rejected in every region. Plain HTTP connections still work.

work_notes.note: The certificates for all three storage endpoint types expired between 20:29 and 20:33 UTC. The same certificates are used in every region and stamp.

Triage done. Two work streams: update the certificate directly on each storage node, and a full service update carrying the new certificates. The renewed certificates were stored in the secret store in early January and included in a planned release, but that release was not flagged as time-critical and was queued behind higher-priority updates. No further expiry alerts were raised after the renewal was stored.
Manual certificate update procedure validated. It was complicated because the node manager keeps returning nodes to their goal state.
Applied the procedure to the storage nodes in one data center.
HTTPS restored in that data center. Rolling out to all storage nodes globally.
All storage nodes updated. HTTPS restored for most customers.
Status dashboard green after extra validation. The full service update with the new certificates is rolling out in parallel to set the final state.

resolution.restoration_action: Updated the certificate on every storage node with a validated manual procedure, followed by a full service update carrying the new certificates.
resolution.confirmed_cause: Service certificates expired because procedures for maintaining and monitoring them broke down; the renewal was not deployed before expiry.
supporting_evidence: Expiry times matched the start of the HTTPS failures
HTTPS recovered once the certificates were replaced on the storage nodes
resolution.remaining_uncertainty: None for the cause. Because the certificates were shared across regions and expired minutes apart, one lapse affected every region at once.
resolution.follow_up: Monitor certificate expiry on production endpoints, not only in the secret store. Treat any production certificate within three months of expiry as a service-impacting event. Automate tracking of releases that carry certificate updates. Spread certificates across regions and time.

expected.suggested_category: any non-empty name that is not an existing taxonomy ID or not_toil

why: Intermittent problem that recovered twice on its own, with no cause identified and no action taken. Nothing to classify and nothing to name. Escalate with no category.

incident.summary: Intermittent access to online resources on wired and wireless networks
incident.reported_symptoms: Access to some internal online resources and some external online resources was intermittent, from both on and off the campus network, on wired and wireless connections. Discovered 11:09 UTC.

work_notes.note: Reports of intermittent access to some internal and some external resources, from wired and wireless clients, on and off the network. Not every resource is affected.
Checked interface error and drop counters on core and edge links: nothing abnormal. No changes on the change calendar in the last 48 hours.
Still intermittent. No pattern found by resource, client type, or location.
Recovered at 14:06 without any action from us. Cause not identified. Continuing to investigate.
Issue resurfaced at 15:00 with the same symptoms.
Recovered again at 15:45, again with no change on our side. Cause still not identified.

resolution.restoration_action: None identified; the service recovered on its own both times.
resolution.remaining_uncertainty: Cause not identified. The issue recovered twice without intervention.
resolution.follow_up: Investigation into the root cause continues.
